quote: Und wie beweist man den Hoppeschen Satz am einfachsten.
english: And how does one prove Hoppe's theorem most simply?
topic: Notes on deriving a theorem from the theorem on perspective triangles without continuity axioms, an analogue of Hoppe's theorem on tetrahedra with equal-area faces in four or more dimensions, and a conjecture on irreducibility of integral polynomials modulo prime powers.

triage.modern_statement: Find the simplest proof of the theorem that if all four faces of a tetrahedron in Euclidean 3-space have equal area, then the faces are congruent. Such a tetrahedron is called equifacial or isosceles, and its opposite edges are equal. Hilbert's note calls this 'Hoppe's theorem'. Today the result is usually credited to Bang (Bang's theorem). The page also asks about an analogue for simplices in four or more dimensions. Strictly speaking the question asks for a simple proof of a known theorem, not for a new result.
triage.answered_by: The theorem was already known when Hilbert wrote the note. In modern literature it is attributed to A. Bang (1897). My sources do not confirm Hilbert's attribution to Hoppe; one source only mentions Hoppe's 1877 examples of Heronian tetrahedra. Several short proofs were published later, including an analytic proof based on Pythagoras' theorem by Hajja and Walker (Journal for Geometry and Graphics, vol. 8, about 2004) and a proof in AwesomeMath's Mathematical Reflections (2021). Klain (arXiv 2112.14918, 2021/2022) extended the theorem: if the faces split into two pairs of equal area, the faces in each pair are congruent. The higher-dimensional analogue is false: equal facet areas do not force congruent facets. This was shown by P. McMullen ('Simplices with equiareal faces', Discrete & Computational Geometry) and is also discussed by Hajja and Walker.

evidence.claim: A note giving an analytic proof, based on Pythagoras' theorem, of Bang's theorem that a tetrahedron whose faces have equal areas has congruent faces. It also shows how to build counterexamples in higher dimensions.
Same paper (ResearchGate copy): none of these statements holds in dimensions above three. For the failure of Bang's theorem in higher dimensions it cites another work.
Expository article titled 'A Tetrahedron Whose Faces Have Equal Area Is "Equifacial"', giving a proof of the theorem.
Klain: if the faces of a tetrahedron can be split into pairs of equal area, the faces in each pair are congruent. He also cites the known result that equal face areas make a tetrahedron isosceles.
Paper on equifacetal simplices that cites McMullen, 'Simplices with equiareal faces' (Discrete & Computational Geometry), and Weissbach for work on simplices whose facets have equal areas.

Journal of Number Theory (2006) paper: Brown proved that a tetrahedron whose four faces have equal area or equal perimeter is of this congruent-face type. In 1877 Hoppe gave eight examples of Heronian tetrahedra of this type.

triage.why: The note asks for a simple proof of a classical fact of solid geometry: a tetrahedron with equal-area faces has congruent faces. Many short proofs have since been published. The question is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or his 24th problem. Related work continues in small expository geometry papers, but it is not an active research area. In four or more dimensions the analogue fails, as McMullen and others showed. Confidence is medium because I could not confirm why Hilbert called it 'Hoppe's theorem'. The only Hoppe link I found is his 1877 Heronian tetrahedra examples. I ran out of searches before I could check Hoppe's papers or McMullen's paper directly.
